docs.title: infersize 📐
docs.text: A deterministic, first-principles analytical capacity planner, VRAM sizing engine, speculative decoding budgeter, and multi-GPU matrix comparator for Large Language Model (LLM) inference.

docs.title: Why infersize?
docs.text:
Deploying large language models often results in expensive surprises: 1. CUDA Out-of-Memory (OOM) crashes after waiting minutes to download 30GB+ model checkpoints. 2. Massive KV-cache footprint at long context lengths (e.g. 32K or 128K) causing serving latency spikes. 3. Speculative Decoding sizing guesses where target and draft models exceed total GPU VRAM headroom. 4. Cloud TCO over-provisioning by renting expensive 8x H100 clusters when a single quantized 4x L40S or A10G pool was mathematically optimal.

infersize solves this by computing exact weight bytes, SwiGLU expansion dimensions, GQA KV-cache scaling, activation tensors, and CUDA runtime context overhead in under 10 milliseconds on your local CPU — before downloading weights or renting clusters.

docs.title: 📦 Quick Installation
docs.text:
# Core CLI engine
pip install infersize

# Or via uv
uv add infersize

# With interactive Streamlit Web Studio
pip install "infersize[ui]"

docs.title: 🚀 Quick Navigation
docs.text:
• VRAM Analytical Physics — First-principles mathematical derivation of parameter counting, SwiGLU, and GQA KV-cache virtual memory.
  • Speculative Sizer — Leviathan speedup derivations (\(S = \frac{1 + \alpha K}{1 + (K+1)/\gamma}\)) and joint target + draft VRAM budgeting.
  • Hardware Zero-OOM Verifier — Real-time NVML hardware querying to verify zero-OOM safety on physical silicon.
  • Web Studio & Streamlit — Launching and using the interactive browser GUI (infersize ui).
  • CLI Reference — Complete command-line manual (estimate, compare, spec, fit, ui).

docs.title: CLI Command Reference
docs.text: infersize provides a command-line interface powered by Typer and Rich.

docs.title: 1. infersize estimate
docs.text:
Estimate VRAM usage, weight footprint, and KV-cache breakdown for a single model: 

infersize estimate --model qwen2.5-7b --quant fp16 --batch-size 4 --context-length 4096

docs.title: Options:
docs.text:
• --model, -m: Model preset name or local path (qwen2.5-0.5b, qwen2.5-7b, llama-3-8b, deepseek-v2-lite).
  • --config, -c: Path to a custom Hugging Face config.json.
  • --quant, -q: Precision (fp16, bf16, int8, int4, fp8, bitnet).
  • --batch-size, -b: Concurrent batch size (default: 1).
  • --context-length, -s: Sequence length in tokens (default: 2048).
  • --tensor-parallel, -tp: Number of GPUs in tensor-parallel group (default: 1).
  • --json-out: Output pure JSON payload for CI/CD scripting.

docs.title: 2. infersize compare
docs.text:
Compare VRAM utilization and determine fit across multiple GPU architectures simultaneously: 

infersize compare --model qwen2.5-7b --quant int4 --gpus rtx3050,rtx4090,a10g,l40s,a100-80gb

docs.title: 3. infersize spec
docs.text:
Calculate joint target + draft model VRAM footprint and theoretical Leviathan speedup: 

infersize spec --target qwen2.5-7b --draft qwen2.5-0.5b --acceptance-rate 0.75 --draft-k 4

docs.title: 4. infersize fit
docs.text:
Verify zero-OOM safety against your current physical workstation hardware: 

infersize fit --model qwen2.5-7b --quant int4 --context-length 4096

docs.title: 5. infersize cost
docs.text:
Calculate cloud TCO, hourly rental expenses, and cost per 1M tokens across providers: 

infersize cost --model qwen2.5-7b --quant fp16 --clouds aws,runpod,lambda

docs.title: 6. infersize report
docs.text:
Generate a comprehensive Architecture Decision RFC document in Markdown or JSON: 

infersize report --model qwen2.5-7b --quant fp16 --output rfc.md

docs.title: 7. infersize ui
docs.text:
Launch the interactive Streamlit Web Studio: 

infersize ui --port 8501

docs.title: Hardware Zero-OOM Verifier (infersize fit)
docs.text:
Theoretical benchmarks assume ideal GPU clusters. In practice, developers test models on their local workstations or laptops (RTX 3050, RTX 4090, Apple Silicon, or CPU RAM).

infersize fit provides a live zero-OOM verification probe that inspects your physical hardware directly.

docs.title: 1. How It Works
docs.text:
1. NVML / CUDA Probe: Queries the active NVIDIA driver and PyTorch CUDA context to determine total VRAM, currently allocated VRAM, and actual unreserved headroom.
  2. System RAM Fallback: If no GPU is present or CUDA is uninitialized, probes total host RAM using OS primitives.
  3. Safety Headroom Analysis:
  4. Evaluates if model weights + KV-cache + activation buffer fits within physical memory.
  5. Emits an amber warning if headroom is \(<15\%\).
  6. Emits a red Out-of-Memory alert if required VRAM exceeds physical capacity.

docs.title: 2. CLI Usage
docs.text:
Verify if a model can run on your current physical machine:

# Verify Qwen 2.5 7B at INT4 precision on your local GPU
infersize fit --model qwen2.5-7b --quant int4 --context-length 4096

docs.title: Speculative Decoding Sizer (infersize spec)
docs.text: Speculative decoding leverages a smaller, high-throughput Draft Model to propose candidate tokens in parallel, which are then verified simultaneously by a larger Target Model in a single batched forward pass.

docs.title: 1. Leviathan Theoretical Speedup Equation
docs.text:
Based on the canonical derivation from Leviathan et al. (Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding), the wall-clock speedup \(S\) achieved over autoregressive generation is given by:

\[S = \frac{1 + \alpha \cdot K}{1 + \frac{K + 1}{\gamma}}\]

Where: * \(K\): Number of speculative draft tokens generated per verification step (lookahead window). * \(\alpha \in [0, 1]\): Empirical token acceptance rate of the draft model. * \(\gamma = \frac{\text{Target Model Step Latency}}{\text{Draft Model Step Latency}}\): Latency ratio between target and draft forward steps.

docs.title: Expected Accepted Tokens Per Step
docs.text: $\(\mathbb{E}[\text{Accepted Tokens}] = \frac{1 - \alpha^{K+1}}{1 - \alpha}\)$ For high acceptance rates (\(\alpha \ge 0.7\)) and optimal draft lengths (\(K \in [3, 6]\)), speculative decoding routinely delivers \(1.8\times\text{--}2.6\times\) empirical speedups.

docs.title: 2. Joint VRAM Memory Budgeting
docs.text:
While speculative decoding improves latency, it places strict memory demands on the accelerator: both models must fit into physical VRAM simultaneously.

\[\text{Total VRAM}_{\text{spec}} = \text{VRAM}_{\text{target}} + \text{VRAM}_{\text{draft}}\]

infersize spec calculates the combined memory footprint across precisions (e.g. Target FP16 + Draft INT4) to ensure the draft model does not trigger a catastrophic CUDA OOM.

docs.title: 3. CLI Example
docs.text:
infersize spec \
  --target qwen2.5-7b --target-quant fp16 \
  --draft qwen2.5-0.5b --draft-quant int4 \
  --gpu a100 --context-length 4096 --acceptance-rate 0.72 --draft-k 4

docs.title: VRAM Analytical Physics & First-Principles Modeling
docs.text: infersize models GPU memory requirements using first-principles analytical formulas calibrated against empirical measurements from modern inference runtimes.

docs.title: 1. Parameter Footprint Derivation
docs.text: For a Transformer model with: * Hidden dimension \(d_{\text{model}}\) * Intermediate MLP dimension \(d_{\text{ffn}}\) * Attention heads \(N_{\text{heads}}\) * Key/Value heads \(N_{\text{kv}}\) (Grouped-Query Attention) * Number of layers \(L\) * Vocabulary size \(V\)

docs.title: Attention Layer Parameters
docs.text: $\(\text{Params}_{\text{attn}} = 2 \cdot d_{\text{model}}^2 + 2 \cdot d_{\text{model}} \cdot (N_{\text{kv}} \cdot D_{\text{head}})\)$ where \(D_{\text{head}} = \frac{d_{\text{model}}}{N_{\text{heads}}}\). In standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA), \(N_{\text{kv}} = N_{\text{heads}}\), giving \(4 \cdot d_{\text{model}}^2\).

docs.title: SwiGLU Feed-Forward Network (FFN)
docs.text:
Standard ReLU/GELU MLPs utilize 2 projection matrices (\(W_{\text{gate}}\) and \(W_{\text{down}}\)): $\(\text{Params}_{\text{FFN}} = 2 \cdot d_{\text{model}} \cdot d_{\text{ffn}}\)$

Modern architectures (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek) utilize gated SwiGLU activations, requiring 3 linear projection matrices (\(W_{\text{gate}}\), \(W_{\text{up}}\), \(W_{\text{down}}\)): $\(\text{Params}_{\text{SwiGLU}} = 3 \cdot d_{\text{model}} \cdot d_{\text{ffn}}\)$

docs.title: Total Parameter Memory
docs.text:
\[\text{Memory}_{\text{weights}} = \text{Total Parameters} \times \text{Bytes Per Weight}\]
  • FP16 / BF16: 2.0 bytes/param
  • INT8 / FP8: 1.0 byte/param
  • INT4 / AWQ / GPTQ: 0.5 bytes/param
  • BitNet 1.58b: ~0.20 bytes/param

docs.title: 2. Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) KV-Cache Footprint
docs.text:
During autoregressive generation, past Key and Value vectors are cached to avoid redundant matrix operations. For sequence length \(S\) and batch size \(B\):

\[\text{KV Bytes Per Token} = 2 \cdot L \cdot N_{\text{kv}} \cdot D_{\text{head}} \cdot \text{dtype\_bytes}\] \[\text{Total KV-Cache Memory} = B \cdot S \cdot \text{KV Bytes Per Token}\]

docs.title: The GQA Memory Compression Advantage
docs.text: Comparing Llama-2-70B (MHA, \(N_{\text{kv}} = 64\)) vs Llama-3-70B (GQA, \(N_{\text{kv}} = 8\)): * MHA (\(N_{\text{kv}} = 64\)): 1.28 MB per token slot across 80 layers. At 32K context (\(B=1\)), KV cache requires 40.96 GB VRAM! * GQA (\(N_{\text{kv}} = 8\)): 0.16 MB per token slot. At 32K context (\(B=1\)), KV cache requires only 5.12 GB VRAM (8x reduction).

docs.title: 3. Activation & Runtime Overhead
docs.text:
1. FlashAttention Peak Activation Memory: $\(\text{Memory}_{\text{act}} \approx B \cdot S \cdot d_{\text{model}} \cdot \text{dtype\_bytes}\)$
  2. CUDA Context & Driver Reserve: $\(\text{Memory}_{\text{CUDA}} \approx 0.6\text{ GB to }1.2\text{ GB}\)$ Pre-allocated by PyTorch and the NVIDIA driver upon initializing the CUDA runtime.
\[\text{Total Required VRAM} = \frac{\text{Memory}_{\text{weights}}}{\text{Tensor Parallel}} + \text{Memory}_{\text{KV}} + \text{Memory}_{\text{act}} + \text{Memory}_{\text{CUDA}}\]

docs.title: Web Studio & Streamlit App (infersize ui)
docs.text:
🚀 Live Cloud Instance: You can test the Web Studio directly in your browser without local installation at infersize.streamlit.app.

For interactive capacity planning, architecture design meetings, and visual RFC reviews, infersize includes a standalone Streamlit Web Studio.

docs.title: 1. Launching the Studio
docs.text:
Ensure the UI extra is installed: 

pip install "infersize[ui]"

Launch the interactive studio: 

# Direct CLI shortcut
infersize ui

# Or via standard streamlit
streamlit run app.py

The browser will open automatically at http://localhost:8501.

docs.title: 2. Interactive Features
docs.text:
• Real-Time Sliders:
  • Adjust sequence length (\(1\text{K}\text{--}128\text{K}\) tokens).
  • Adjust concurrency batch size (\(1\text{--}64\) active streams).
  • Toggle Tensor Parallelism (\(TP = 1, 2, 4, 8\)).
  • Change weight precision (FP16, INT8, INT4, FP8, BitNet).
  • Multi-GPU Comparison Matrix:
  • Live comparison table across RTX 3050, RTX 4090, A10G, L40S, A100 (40GB/80GB), and H100.
  • Automatic badge indicators: [FIT], [OOM], and [RIGHT-SIZED].
  • Architecture RFC Exporter:
  • One-click download of a production-ready Markdown report (architecture_rfc.md) detailing memory bounds, roofline decode throughput, and cloud TCO estimates ($ / 1M tokens) for engineering stakeholders.
